reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: Classically presents with bone fragility and recurrent fractures from little or no trauma, often prompting consideration of non-accidental injury which must be excluded
Most cases result from dominant pathogenic variants in COL1A1 or COL1A2 affecting type I collagen quantity or structure, though recessive forms involving collagen-processing genes exist
Extraskeletal features frequently include blue or grey sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, ligamentous laxity, and progressive conductive or mixed hearing loss
The Sillence classification (types I-IV, with expanded modern subtypes) ranges from mild (type I) through perinatally lethal (type II) to progressively deforming (type III)
Radiographs show generalised osteopenia, thin cortices, gracile or bowed long bones, wormian bones in the skull, and vertebral compression
Bisphosphonates are used to reduce fracture frequency and bone pain, alongside physiotherapy, orthopaedic fracture and deformity management, and audiology surveillance
Basilar invagination is an important late craniocervical complication in severe deforming disease
reference.pathophysiology: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a heritable disorder of connective tissue in which abnormal type I collagen, the principal protein of bone matrix, leads to reduced bone mass and mechanical fragility. Most patients carry dominant variants in COL1A1 or COL1A2; null variants reduce the amount of otherwise normal collagen and cause milder disease, whereas variants that distort the collagen triple helix produce a more severe dominant-negative effect. Rarer recessive forms disrupt genes involved in collagen folding, post-translational modification, or bone mineralisation. The resulting defective matrix impairs bone strength and also affects other collagen-rich tissues such as sclera, dentine, and the middle ear ossicles.
additionalDifferentials: Menkes disease and other collagen or copper metabolism disorders
additionalInvestigations: Skeletal survey to characterise fracture pattern, bowing, wormian bones, and vertebral changes
Molecular genetic testing of COL1A1/COL1A2 and, if negative, an extended skeletal dysplasia/recessive OI gene panel
Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry to quantify bone mineral density
Audiological assessment for conductive or mixed hearing loss
Craniocervical imaging in severe disease to detect basilar invagination
redFlags: Multiple fractures at different healing stages requiring careful differentiation from non-accidental injury
Progressive spinal deformity with restrictive respiratory compromise
Neurological signs suggesting basilar invagination or brainstem compression
Perinatal presentation with a small deformed thorax and multiple in-utero fractures suggesting a lethal form
reference.prognosis: Prognosis spans from a near-normal lifespan and function in mild type I disease to perinatal lethality in type II. Severe deforming forms carry lifelong mobility limitation, and outcome is strongly influenced by respiratory reserve and craniocervical complications.
pitfalls: Attributing fractures solely to abuse, or conversely dismissing genuine inflicted injury as OI, without appropriate multidisciplinary assessment
Relying on sclerae colour alone, as blue sclerae are non-specific and may be absent in some types
Overlooking hearing loss and dental disease, which need proactive surveillance
Failing to monitor for basilar invagination in progressively deforming disease
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Bisphosphonate antiresorptive therapy to reduce fracture frequency and bone pain in moderate-to-severe disease
Orthopaedic fracture management and intramedullary rodding to stabilise and correct deformity in bowed or repeatedly fracturing long bones
Physiotherapy, rehabilitation and mobility aids to build strength and maximise function and independence
Audiological surveillance for conductive or mixed hearing loss and dental care for dentinogenesis imperfecta
Monitoring with bone densitometry and, in severe disease, craniocervical imaging for basilar invagination
Coordinated care through a multidisciplinary bone and skeletal-dysplasia team
Genetic counselling and family assessment given dominant COL1A1/COL1A2 inheritance and rarer recessive forms
